aiAgentFacts.fact: In UK primary care during 2019, dogs aged 6 to under 9 years, male neutered and female neutered dogs, insured dogs, and Rottweiler, Bichon Frise and West Highland White Terrier breeds had increased odds of unilateral cranial cruciate ligament rupture diagnosis.

Insured status increased the odds of BOTH diagnosis and surgical management. Insurance cannot affect ligament biology, so this is an ascertainment and decision effect, and it implies every other risk factor here is subject to detection bias to an unknown degree.
The Bichon Frise appearing among the most predisposed breeds alongside the Rottweiler indicates this is not exclusively a large-breed condition.
Insured dogs and dogs weighing 20 kg or more had increased odds of surgical management; dogs aged 9 years or over and dogs with one non-orthopaedic comorbidity had reduced odds.
The management findings describe what practices decided, NOT what produced better outcomes — no outcome of surgical versus non-surgical management is reported.
Among 831 dogs weighing at least 15 kg that were 8 years or older at first rupture, 19.1% (95% CI 16.6-22.0%) subsequently ruptured the contralateral ligament, at a median of 12.9 months.
The contralateral figure applies to older medium-to-large dogs specifically and is described by its authors as lower than previously reported; it must not be applied to young or small dogs.
Age and breed — Golden Retrievers and Labrador Retrievers — were significantly associated with contralateral rupture in that cohort.

historyQuestions: Not prescribed by either paper. The intermittent character of cruciate lameness supports asking when the limp began, which limb, and whether it has waxed and waned — an apparent recovery followed by relapse is characteristic.
redFlags: Not addressed — neither study identifies red-flag findings or urgency thresholds.
differentialDiagnosesMentioned: Not addressed — the cohort study identifies verified incident cases and does not evaluate other causes of hind-limb lameness.
recommendedDiagnosticWorkups: Not evaluated. Cases were identified from verified clinical records; diagnosis in practice rests on orthopaedic examination of the stifle, which neither paper assesses for accuracy.

limitations: Record-based design measures diagnosis, not disease: insured status raising the odds proves detection bias is operating, and its magnitude for other risk factors is unknown
The neutering association cannot be separated from body composition, owner type or veterinary attendance frequency in this design
No population prevalence, no severity grading and no clinical outcome are reported
Management findings describe practice decisions rather than comparative effectiveness of surgical versus conservative treatment
Single country (UK), single year (2019), unilateral cases only
The contralateral rupture figure comes from a narrower population (>=15 kg, >=8 years at first rupture) and a different caseload; it does not transfer to young or small dogs
Both papers are retrospective; neither followed dogs prospectively from a defined starting point
